title: Tell me about yourself — give a short 2-minute story: who you are, what you do, what you have done, and what you want to do next.
shortTitle: Tell me about yourself — a short 2-minute story

s1_definition.profdef: The "Tell me about yourself" question is an open behavioral prompt that expects a concise, structured professional narrative — typically present (who you are and what you do now), past (what you have built and the impact), and future (what you want to do next). A senior answer is a tight two-minute story anchored on measurable achievements in your domain, not a recital of your resume line by line.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine Rajesh walks into National Bank of India to open a relationship as a new corporate client. The manager does not want Rajesh to read out every bank statement he has ever had. The manager wants a short story: "I am a software engineer, today I run the payments platform, last year I cut settlement failures in half, and next I want to own fraud detection." That short, structured story is exactly what "Tell me about yourself" wants.
s1_definition.oneliner: Present, past, future — a two-minute story anchored on one or two measurable banking achievements, not a resume read-out.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The "Tell me about yourself" question is an open behavioral prompt that expects a concise, structured professional narrative — typically present (who you are and what you do now), past (what you have built and the impact), and future (what you want to do next). A senior answer is a tight two-minute story anchored on measurable achievements in your domain, not a recital of your resume line by line.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine Rajesh walks into National Bank of India to open a relationship as a new corporate client. The manager does not want Rajesh to read out every bank statement he has ever had. The manager wants a short story: "I am a software engineer, today I run the payments platform, last year I cut settlement failures in half, and next I want to own fraud detection." That short, structured story is exactly what "Tell me about yourself" wants.

**One line to remember:** Present, past, future — a two-minute story anchored on one or two measurable banking achievements, not a resume read-out.

sections.s2_technical:
The best mental model for this question is the STAR framework adapted into a narrative arc. STAR stands for Situation, Task, Action, Result. For "Tell me about yourself", you compress many little STAR stories into one headline STAR: the Situation is where you work and what the system does, the Task is your role and responsibility, the Action is the signature thing you built, and the Result is the measurable number you moved.

The structure that works is three blocks. The present block states your current role in one or two sentences: "I am a backend engineer on the payments platform at a bank, working in Java and Spring Boot." In code terms this is like the class declaration — it tells the listener what type of engineer you are. For example, a one-line self-summary in a profile object would look like `Candidate me = Candidate.builder().role("Senior Backend Engineer").domain("Payments").stack("Java 17, Spring Boot, Kafka").build();` which captures the headline before any detail.

The past block is your proof. Pick one achievement and state it as a result with a number. For example, "I rebuilt our fund-transfer service and reduced settlement failures from three percent to under half a percent." If you were asked to represent that improvement in code you might log it as `log.info(() -> "Settlement failure rate improved: " + before + "% to " + after + "%")` so the listener hears the measurable delta, which is what makes a senior answer land.

The future block connects your past to their job. "I want to go deeper into real-time fraud detection, which is why this role interests me." This is the part most candidates skip, and it is the part that signals direction.

A senior nuance is to keep it to two minutes and to avoid personal biography — where you were born, your hobbies, your full education history — unless it directly supports the professional story. Another nuance is to tailor the one achievement you lead with to the job you are interviewing for: for a payments role, lead with a payments result; for a trading role, lead with a trading result.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The interviewer asks a vague, open question and most candidates ramble for five minutes listing every project. This is exactly how an unstructured log file behaves — lots of lines, no signal, impossible to find the one event that matters. The STAR narrative fixes this by emitting a few structured, high-signal events in a fixed order.

Problem 2 — The candidate states achievements without numbers: "I improved the transfer service." This is like a log line that says "something happened" with no values — the reader learns nothing. The fix is to always attach a measurable before-and-after, exactly like logging a balance before and after a debit.

To make this concrete and runnable, we will build a small demo that models a candidate pitch as structured data and prints it as a clean, two-minute narrative with timestamps and levels, the same way a real service prints an audit trail. The demo has a `CandidateProfile` class holding the present, past, and future blocks, a `PitchService` that renders the narrative and validates that the past block contains a measurable result, and a `PitchDemo` main class that wires them together using the standard National Bank of India characters Rajesh and Priya as example achievements. The demo will show how a structured pitch is easy to read, and it will warn (just like a real validator) when an achievement has no number attached.

```bash
# Compile all sources into the out directory
javac -d out src/main/java/com/bank/pitch/PitchDemo.java \
             src/main/java/com/bank/pitch/model/CandidateProfile.java \

```
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a CandidateProfile with a present block, a past block mentioning the transfer service between Rajesh and Priya, a future block about fraud detection, and the numbers 3.0 and 0.4 for the failure rate before and after.

Step 1: The main method builds the CandidateProfile object. All three text blocks and the two numbers now live together inside one object in memory.

Step 2: PitchService receives the profile and first prints the present block. The data is unchanged; it is only read and emitted as a log line.

Step 3: The service calls hasMeasurableResult, which compares 3.0 against 0.4. They differ, so the method returns true. This is the validation gate that separates a strong answer from a vague one.

Step 4: Because the result is measurable, the service computes the delta of 2.6 percentage points and prints the past block with that number attached. The stored numbers do not change; the delta is a derived value.

Step 5: The future block is printed, connecting the past achievement to the target role. Finally a completion line is logged.

```
INFO: PRESENT: I am a senior backend engineer on the payments platform at National Bank of India, working in Java 17, Spring Boot and Kafka.
INFO: PAST: I rebuilt the fund-transfer service that moves money between Rajesh's savings account and Priya's current account; I cut settlement failures from 3% to 0.4%. (improvement: 2.6 percentage points)
INFO: FUTURE: Next I want to go deeper into real-time fraud detection, which is exactly why this role interests me.
INFO: Pitch complete — delivered in under two minutes.
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Interviewer: "Tell me about yourself"
    │
    ▼
  CandidateProfile { present, past, future, before=3.0, after=0.4 }
    │
    ▼
  PitchService.renderPitch()
    ├─ print PRESENT  ────────────→ "senior backend engineer, payments"
    ├─ hasMeasurableResult()?
    │     ├─ true  → print PAST + delta (2.6 pts)
    │     └─ false → WARN "add a number"
    └─ print FUTURE  ─────────────→ "fraud detection"
    │
    ▼
  Two-minute structured narrative (present → past → future)
```

sections.s5d_lld:
```
  ═══ LLD — Candidate Pitch (STAR narrative) ═══

  ┌─ Design intent ────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Single Responsibility: CandidateProfile holds data,         │
  │   PitchService renders/validates — two jobs, two classes.   │
  │ STAR mapping: present=Situation+Task, past=Action+Result,   │
  │   future=forward link to the role.                          │
  │ Validation rule: an achievement must move a number.         │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌───────────────────────────────┐        ┌───────────────────────────┐
  │        CandidateProfile       │        │        PitchService       │
  │  - present: String            │◇──────▶│  - log: Logger            │
  │  - past: String               │  uses  │  + renderPitch(profile)   │
  │  - future: String             │        │     prints present/past/  │
  │  - resultBefore: double       │        │     future, warns if no   │
  │  - resultAfter: double        │        │     measurable result     │
  │  + hasMeasurableResult():bool │        └───────────────────────────┘
  └───────────────────────────────┘

  Call chain:
  1. PitchDemo.main() builds CandidateProfile
  2. PitchService.renderPitch(profile)
  3.   print present
  4.   profile.hasMeasurableResult() → true
  5.   print past + delta → print future
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
I am a senior backend engineer with several years of experience building payment and banking systems in Java, Spring Boot, and Kafka. Right now I work on the core payments platform at a bank, where I own the fund-transfer service that moves money between customer accounts safely and reliably. My day-to-day is designing APIs, making transactional code correct under load, and keeping latency and failure rates low because this is money and mistakes are expensive.

The achievement I am most proud of is rebuilding our fund-transfer service. It used to have a settlement failure rate of around three percent, which meant a lot of stuck transfers and a lot of customer complaints. I redesigned the retry and reconciliation flow, added idempotency so repeated requests could not double-debit an account, and improved the database transaction boundaries. The failure rate dropped to under half a percent, which directly reduced customer complaints and manual reconciliation work for the operations team.

Looking forward, I want to go deeper into real-time fraud detection, because that is where payments engineering gets genuinely hard and genuinely valuable — you are making a decision in milliseconds that protects a customer's money. That is exactly why this role interests me, since it sits right at the intersection of high-throughput payments and fraud.

The reason I structure my answer this way is that it follows a present, past, future arc and anchors the past on a measurable result, not a vague claim. I lead with who I am and what I do, I prove it with one achievement that has a real number behind it, and I connect that to what I want to do next and to your role. That is the difference between a two-minute story an interviewer remembers and a five-minute resume read-out they tune out of.

---

keyPoints: STAR method: Situation, Task, Action, Result
2-minute story: current role, key achievements, why this role
Focus on: technical skills, leadership, impact
Tailor to the company and role you are interviewing for
